sections.overview: Ochlerotatus sticticus, also widely called *Aedes sticticus*, is a floodwater mosquito whose larvae can become abundant after river or seasonal flooding. Both genus combinations occur in the literature.
sections.identification: It is described as a relatively large and aggressive floodplain mosquito; close examination with an identification key is needed to distinguish similar species.
sections.habitat: Its eggs are laid on damp ground in flood-prone meadows and woodland, then hatch when rising water inundates them. Larvae develop in temporary pools left by rain or river floods.
sections.diet: Adult females take blood meals from mammals, including people and livestock. Larvae feed in water, but their exact food has not been characterised for this species.
sections.behavior: Its dormant eggs can persist through dry periods, and flooding triggers synchronized larval emergence; adult numbers may therefore rise sharply after suitable floods.
sections.reproduction: The species overwinters as eggs in damp habitat. In northern Italy, the main adult emergence was observed in April or May, with timing varying according to egg submersion and temperature.
sections.ecology: In parts of Sweden it is an important nuisance species during flood outbreaks. That local impact does not mean every population is abundant or medically important.
sections.conservation: The sources consulted document its ecology and local nuisance impacts, but do not provide a global population estimate or conservation assessment.
